hops.title: A giraffe's five-meter nerve
hops.text: A giraffe's voice box sits just below its skull, a short distance from the brainstem. On the left side, the nerve route that runs it takes the long way: down the neck, around the aorta near the heart, and back up to the throat. In the largest giraffes, whose necks reach 2.4 meters, that nerve pathway approaches five meters. Put five meters into the formula above and a soluble protein would need almost 40,000 years to drift from one end to the other. The sauropod Supersaurus probably stretched the same detour past 28 meters, more than a million years of drift. Across a route that long, cargo needs active transport.

sources.citation: Wedel, M. J. (2012). A monument of inefficiency: The presumed course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in sauropod dinosaurs. Acta Palaeontologica Polonica, 57(2), 251–256.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A giraffe bending its very long neck toward low acacia branches on a sunny savanna.
image.caption: A giraffe's voice-box nerve runs about five meters, far too far for a signal to drift.

hops.title: Tracing nerves with a horseradish enzyme
hops.text: In 1971, Krister Kristensson and Yngve Olsson used an unlikely laboratory tool: horseradish peroxidase, an enzyme from horseradish root. They injected it into leg or tongue muscle in separate rodent studies, then stained the tissue for peroxidase activity. The color appeared in motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord and brainstem, far from the injection sites. The axon terminals had taken it up and carried it back. The next year, Jennifer and Matthew LaVail injected it into a chick's visual brain center and timed retinal axons carrying it home at about 72 millimeters a day. For decades, it was neuroanatomy's standard way to trace circuits in reverse.

sources.citation: Lanciego, J. L., & Wouterlood, F. G. (2020). Neuroanatomical tract-tracing techniques that did go viral. Brain Structure and Function, 225(4), 1193–1224 (citing Kristensson & Olsson, 1971).
LaVail, J. H., & LaVail, M. M. (1972). Retrograde axonal transport in the central nervous system. Science, 176(4042), 1416–1417.
Kristensson, K., & Olsson, Y. (1971). Retrograde axonal transport of protein. Brain Research, 29(2), 363-365 (PubMed record, MeSH: Mice, Muscles, Spinal Cord, Motor Neurons).
Kristensson, K., & Olsson, Y. (1971). Uptake and retrograde axonal transport of peroxidase in hypoglossal neurons. Acta Neuropathologica (PubMed record, MeSH: Mice).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fresh horseradish root beside a classic microscope and a small glass bottle on a wooden lab bench.
image.caption: Axons carry a horseradish-root enzyme back to their cell bodies, so it became a tool for mapping wiring in reverse.

hops.title: Tap your big toe
hops.text: Tap your big toe on the floor. Take a sensory axon about a meter long, from your foot to its cell body beside the lower spine. The tap travels along it as an electrical relay, regenerated again and again along the axon. A study of a sensory nerve on the outer foot measured about 50 meters per second; at that speed, the relay covers the meter in about 20 milliseconds. Now suppose a chemical package left the same toe at the same instant, riding dynein at the lesson's one micrometer per second. It would arrive in almost twelve days. The relay is about fifty million times faster.

sources.citation: Ahn, S., Riccio, A., & Ginty, D. D. (2000). Spatial considerations for stimulus-dependent transcription in neurons. Annual Review of Physiology, 62, 803–823.

Luigetti, M., Guglielmino, V., Romozzi, M., et al. (2022). Nerve conduction studies of dorsal sural nerve: Normative data and its potential application in ATTRv pre-symptomatic subjects. Brain Sciences, 12(8), 1037.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A seated student tapping one sneakered toe on the floor while looking down at a wristwatch.
image.caption: Over one meter, an electrical relay takes milliseconds; at one micrometer per second, dynein cargo takes almost twelve days.
